title: Japji 16–19, whole
hook: the countless, and the Name through letters
tomorrow: after the countless, what does the Japji say washes a mind clean?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Japji 8: listen, trust, in that order. Six lines this week: freedom for all, a new month, lived, not just learned, the same words, deeper, walk in the order, and listen, trust.

Ever tried counting the stars on a clear night and given up somewhere past the first handful? Pauri seventeen of the Japji opens with a word that gives up counting on purpose: asankh, countless. Asankh jap, asankh bhaau: countless prayers, countless loves. Pauri eighteen turns it around: countless fools, countless thieves. Pauri nineteen: countless names, countless places. What do you do with a list that can't end?
screen: `STARS PAST THE FIRST HANDFUL.` → `ASANKH: COUNTLESS.` → `A LIST THAT CAN'T END.`

segments.voice: Pauri sixteen sets the stage: panch parvaan panch pardhaan, the chosen ones are accepted and honored. And the old picture of a bull holding up the earth gets a new reading: the bull is dharam, righteousness, the son of compassion, held in place by the thread of contentment. Then the counting starts, and breaks. Countless devotions, countless scholars. Countless cruel ones too, and Guru Nanak, after naming them, calls himself the lowly one, as if setting himself inside the list. Then pauri nineteen turns: akharee naam, akharee saalaah. Through letters, the Name; through letters, praise. A creation too big to count is still sung in letters, the small marks this year began with. Each of these pauris closes on the same refrain, in paraphrase: what power have I to describe your creation? Whatever pleases you is good; you are forever, Formless One.
screen: `THE BULL IS DHARAM.` · `ASANKH: THE COUNT BREAKS.` · `NANAK, THE LOWLY, IN THE LIST.` · `THROUGH LETTERS, THE NAME.` · then, large: `THE COUNTLESS.`

segments.voice: Count slowly on your fingers, one breath for each thing you're grateful for today: a person, a meal, a quiet minute, anything at all. When your fingers run out, keep going without counting, and notice that the list doesn't end.
Japji 16. Pauris sixteen to nineteen, read whole: the bull that is dharam, the countless, and the Name sung through letters.
Keep this one: the countless, sung through a handful of letters. Four of the summit, and a week counted.

chat.says: bebe & i tried listing what i'm taking to college. gave up halfway. she just said 'asankh' and laughed. huh?
options: Asankh means countless. Some lists can't end; the Japji says so, then simply praises.
Asankh means a short list, so she's telling you to pack light, just a few things.
It's a word for clutter. The Japji warns against owning too many things.
